vignette:
The Weight of the Ward

Priya is thirty-two years old, a registered nurse who has worked in critical care for nearly a decade. She grew up in a close-knit Tamil family in the East Midlands, the eldest daughter of parents who sacrificed a great deal to see her become what her mother still calls "our doctor-nurse." She was good at her job — methodical, warm, the kind of nurse who remembered which patients liked the blinds open in the morning and which ones needed silence.

In the spring of 2020, her hospital's intensive care unit was overwhelmed within a matter of days. She describes it now as watching the ward transform into something unrecognizable — beds pushed into corridors, colleagues she had worked alongside for years redeployed or falling sick themselves, and a relentless, grinding shortage of everything: PPE, ventilators, time. She watched people die alone, holding iPads so that families could say goodbye through screens. She held the hands of patients who were terrified, knowing she had perhaps four minutes before she had to move to the next bed. One night, during a shift that stretched past fourteen hours, a patient she had been caring for closely — a fifty-eight-year-old man who had shown her photographs of his grandchildren — deteriorated rapidly. There were not enough staff. She made decisions she was not qualified to make alone. He died before the registrar arrived. She went home, showered, and returned the next morning.

She did not stop working. That, she says, was the problem. She kept going for another eight months before her body made the decision her mind refused to. She began having what she initially dismissed as panic attacks — sudden, crushing sensations of heat and noise, the smell of the unit flooding back without warning, her heart slamming against her ribs as though she were still standing at that bedside. She stopped sleeping properly. When she did sleep, she returned to the ward in her dreams, except in the dreams she is always too slow, always arriving a moment too late, always watching the monitor flatline as she reaches for it.

Now, two years on, Priya is back at work in a different unit — surgical, quieter, nothing like ICU — but the distance has not brought the relief she expected. She avoids the east wing of the hospital entirely because it shares a corridor with the old ICU. She has rearranged her commute so she does not pass the staff entrance she used during that period. When an alarm sounds anywhere on the ward — even a routine call bell — she feels her body brace as though for impact, a tightening across her chest and shoulders that takes minutes to release. She is hypervigilant with her patients in ways that her colleagues sometimes find difficult to understand, checking observations more frequently than necessary, catastrophising minor changes in their condition.

Outside of work, Priya has pulled inward. She declined her cousin's wedding last year, unable to face the noise and the expectation of happiness. She tells her mother she is "just tired." She has not told her family what the unit was like during those months, partly because she does not have words for it, and partly because she does not want to become, in their eyes, someone who is broken. Her parents' pride in her is something she carries carefully, like something fragile. She does not want to set it down.

She describes a persistent, low-level sense of guilt that she cannot reason her way out of — a conviction that she should have done more, been faster, been better. She knows, intellectually, that the system failed. She does not feel it intellectually. She feels it in her body, in the four o'clock wakefulness, in the way she still sometimes stands at a patient's bedside and sees, briefly, a different face looking back at her.

She came to therapy, she says, because she is tired of being afraid of her own workplace. She wants her job back — the version of it she loved.
